questions.prompt: In the cardiac ventricle, the Phase 1 initial repolarization is caused by a transient outward potassium current and the inactivation of sodium channels.
The plateau phase (Phase 2) of the ventricular action potential results from an electrical balance where the inward calcium current is equal to the outward potassium current.
According to hemodynamics, the linear velocity of blood flow is directly proportional to the total cross-sectional area of the vascular segment.

Activation of the sympathetic nervous system increases the conduction velocity in the atrioventricular (AV) node primarily by increasing the inward calcium current during the action potential upstroke.
The absolute refractory period (ARP) of a cardiac cell ends when the cell has repolarized to a membrane potential of approximately -50 mV.
Parasympathetic stimulation of the sinoatrial (SA) node decreases heart rate by increasing the probability that "funny" (If) channels are in the open state.
In vascular smooth muscle, the phosphorylation of myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) by cAMP-dependent protein kinase results in muscle contraction.
The Law of Laplace for a sphere indicates that wall stress is inversely proportional to the thickness of the ventricular wall.
During isovolumetric ventricular contraction, both the atrioventricular valves and the semilunar valves are closed while ventricular pressure rises.
A positive inotropic effect, such as that produced by digitalis, causes an increase in the ejection fraction and a decrease in the end-systolic volume.
The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure curve is caused by the brief retrograde flow of blood toward the heart immediately following aortic valve closure.
In the baroreceptor reflex, a decrease in mean arterial pressure leads to a decrease in the firing rate of the carotid sinus nerve.
Angiotensin II increases blood pressure by acting as a vasodilator on peripheral arterioles.
An increase in the resistance of the arterioles (TPR) results in a clockwise rotation of the vascular function curve on a cardiac output graph.
Myocardial oxygen consumption is more significantly increased by "pressure work" (internal work against high afterload) than by "volume work" (cardiac output).
In the coronary circulation, the primary mechanism of vasodilation in response to increased myocardial activity is the release of local metabolites such as adenosine.
The "central command" in the response to exercise originates in the motor cortex and initiates sympathetic outflow before any metabolic changes occur in the muscles.
During acute hemorrhage, the resulting increase in sympathetic activity leads to the constriction of arterioles in the brain and heart to preserve total peripheral resistance.
The mean systemic filling pressure is an experimental value that represents the pressure in the circulation when the heart is stopped and the blood has redistributed.
In the kidneys, sympathetic stimulation increases the glomerular filtration rate by dilating the afferent arterioles.
A decrease in arterial compliance, common in elderly patients, results in a decreased pulse pressure.
In the SA node, Phase 0 is caused by an inward sodium current through fast voltage-gated sodium channels.
Autoregulation in the cerebral circulation is primarily regulated by the local partial pressure of carbon dioxide (P_(CO2)).
During exercise, the increase in heart rate and contractility is accompanied by a decrease in venous return due to skeletal muscle relaxation.
The fourth heart sound (S4) is typically heard during the rapid ventricular filling phase of diastole.
In the heart, the effective refractory period (ERP) is slightly longer than the absolute refractory period (ARP) because it includes the time required to generate a conducted action potential.
Stimulation of beta-2 adrenergic receptors on skeletal muscle arterioles produces vasoconstriction.
Edema is more likely to form when there is a decrease in the capillary filtration coefficient (Kf).
The PR interval on an ECG correlates with the conduction time through the atrioventricular (AV) node.
Arginine vasopressin (ADH) increases total peripheral resistance by binding to V2 receptors in vascular smooth muscle.
The Cushing reaction involves systemic hypertension and tachycardia in response to increased intracranial pressure.
Mean arterial pressure is calculated as the simple arithmetic average of the systolic and diastolic pressures.
An increase in contractility shifts the cardiac function curve upward and to the left.
During the "reduced ventricular ejection" phase, aortic pressure begins to fall because the rate of blood "running off" to the periphery exceeds the rate of ejection.
The filtration of fluid out of the capillaries is generally higher at the arteriolar end because the capillary hydrostatic pressure is maximal at that point.
Sympathetic stimulation of the heart increases the rate of Phase 4 depolarization in the SA node by increasing the "funny" current (If).
Phospholamban, when phosphorylated by protein kinase A, increases the activity of the Ca^(2+)-ATPase (SERCA) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
A decrease in blood viscosity, such as in anemia, leads to a decrease in the Reynolds number and a lower probability of turbulent flow.
In a series arrangement of blood vessels, the total resistance is calculated as the sum of the individual resistances of each segment.
Left ventricular stroke work is defined as the product of stroke volume and the mean aortic pressure.
The ejection fraction is calculated as the stroke volume divided by the end-systolic volume.
Activation of the Bainbridge reflex causes a decrease in heart rate when atrial pressure increases.
In the fetal circulation, pulmonary blood flow is significantly higher than aortic blood flow.
Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) causes vasodilation and increases sodium excretion by the kidneys, which serves to reduce blood volume.
In the Starling equation, a positive value for fluid movement (Jv) indicates that net absorption of fluid into the capillary is occurring.
The presence of an arteriovenous (AV) shunt or fistula leads to an increase in total peripheral resistance.
During isovolumetric ventricular relaxation, the ventricular volume remains constant while the ventricular pressure drops below the aortic pressure.
Most of the total blood volume in the cardiovascular system is found within the systemic arteries at any given time.
High levels of extracellular potassium (hyperkalemia) can lead to cardiac arrest in diastole by depolarizing the resting membrane potential and inactivating sodium channels.
The "v" wave on a jugular venous pulse tracing corresponds to the period of atrial contraction.
